SM17A-A2.free_elimination: Parity. The condition reads c = 2*f(1) + 5, and f(1) is an integer whatever c is, so c must be ODD. That strikes '6'. No sign, bound or echo strike beyond it: all four options are integers, -21 is the lone negative but it is a distractor, and 59 is not a printed number.
SM17A-A2.note: Labelled hard; it is a two-line vertex reading plus a linear equation in c, which is a real module-2 medium. Distractor rationales are all genuine misreadings (sign on the leading coefficient, mis-scoped 'more than', mis-signed vertex) and each distractor_solve is an independent expression, not a hardcode.

SM17A-A3.free_elimination: None found at the option-set level. The nearest thing is a shortcut, not a strike: a*b^2 = 45 with a,b positive integers admits only (5,3) and (45,1), and b=1 is killed by the growth, so the key is reachable from f(2) alone and f(5)=1215 is redundant. That is a construction weakness, not an elimination - it does not tell you which listed option to discard without doing the factorisation.
SM17A-A3.note: Ratio-of-two-outputs is the most routine exponential item there is; 'medium' overstates it for the hard route. Distractors are well chosen (product instead of sum, one power instead of two, output read as coefficient). The redundancy of the second datum is the only thing I would change if this were re-authored.

SM17A-A4.free_elimination: Closure/product structure. The stem asks for ab, a product of two constants that must come out of {3, 5, 12} (the numbers the given form and the original function supply). 15 = 3*5, 36 = 3*12, 60 = 12*5 are all such products; 17 is prime and is a SUM (12+5), so it is strikeable as the wrong kind of quantity. Printed-number echo is present throughout - every option is a combination of 3, 5 and 12 - which is what keeps the echo from favouring the key.
SM17A-A4.note: Labelled easy; inverting a rational function and matching two constants is a module-2 medium, not easy. The solve snippet reconstructs a and b by sampling f rather than by inverting symbolically, which is an independent path and lands on 60.

SM17A-A5.free_elimination: None found. Nothing about the option set separates 29/40/45/53 before the numerator is expanded: the positivity bound that would strike 29 and 40 (both contributions to b are positive because of the double negative, so b = 40 and a + b > 40) IS the expansion, and the sign handling it rests on is exactly the skill the 29 distractor tests. Parity does not cut (three odds, one even, and the even is a distractor). The explanation's own claim that neither constant is readable by inspection holds up.
SM17A-A5.note: Clean item. The three distractors cover the three real failure modes independently (double-negative, added instead of subtracted, reported b alone) and each distractor_solve is a genuine mis-execution rather than a restated literal.

SM17A-A6.free_elimination: None found, and I checked the residue channel specifically. Evaluating the division identity at x = 1 gives 3(2 + m + n) + (p + q) = 7, so m+n+p+q = 1 - 2(m+n) and the answer is forced ODD - all four options (-1, 5, 9, 17) are odd, so the parity filter eliminates nothing. No option is a printed coefficient, and the lone negative (-1) is a distractor.
SM17A-A6.note: Best-constructed item in the batch: the option set survives the parity filter that its own structure generates. Only blemish is that the three distractor_solve snippets hardcode m, n, p, q rather than re-running the division with the slip in place, so they document the error instead of reproducing it. The key's own solve does run a real division loop.

SM17A-A7.free_elimination: TWO strikes, not the one the explanation concedes. (1) Parity: y1 + y2 = 2(x1 + x2) + 8, and x1 + x2 = -b is an integer because the difference quadratic is monic with integer coefficients, so the answer is EVEN - that strikes -1 with no arithmetic at all. (2) The explanation's own strike: -14 is the bare difference of two printed constants (-10 and 4) offered as a sum of two y-values. A solver holding options only is left choosing between 6 and 10, i.e. 50%. The explanation asserts '-14 is the one strikeable option ... inside tolerance'; the parity strike is independent of it and also free, so the recorded tolerance is understated.
SM17A-A7.note: Mathematics is right and the Vieta path is the intended one (roots are irrational, so substitution is genuinely blocked). Re-option rather than drop: replace -1 with an even wrong-variable value, or change the line so the y-sum is odd, so the two free strikes do not stack into a coin flip.

SM17A-A8.free_elimination: None found; the residue channel was checked and is closed by construction. p(3) = 42 + 3(3a + b), so the answer is necessarily divisible by 3, and all four options (-42, 18, 30, 66) are divisible by 3 (indeed all four are even as well). No option echoes a printed number, and the lone negative is a distractor.
SM17A-A8.note: Genuinely hard and clean: factor theorem, a 2x2 system, then remainder theorem. The '66' distractor_solve hardcodes a = 6, b = -10 (the explanation is honest that this pair satisfies neither condition), so that one snippet documents rather than derives; the other two run the real system.

SM17A-B1.free_elimination: Residue, two struck. The axis sits midway between -2 and 3, so the vertex-to-zero distance is 2.5 and its square carries a denominator of 4: 25a/4 = 150 forces 4 | a. Of the options only 24 and 60 are multiples of 4, so 6 and 25 fall with no arithmetic beyond reading the midpoint off the zeros. It does NOT isolate the key - 60 survives, which is what keeps this inside tolerance. (I initially expected a full isolation here; 60 = 4*15 refutes it.)
SM17A-B1.note: Acceptable as it stands, but the two survivors are the key and the 'never squared the distance' distractor, so the item degrades to 50% for a solver who gets the /4 insight and stops. If it is cheap to re-option, make 6 and 25 into multiples of 4 (e.g. 4 and 100) so the residue channel is closed the way A6 and A8 close theirs.

SM17A-B2.free_elimination: None found - and I verified the perfect-square filter independently rather than taking the explanation's word for it. x - 16 over the four options is 9, 16, 25, 49: ALL FOUR are perfect squares, so the filter strikes nothing and the key is not isolated by it. The magnitude bound is closed too: x = 21 + 4*sqrt(x-16) > 21 holds for all of 25, 32, 41, 65, and the extraneous root x = 17 (which would be freely strikeable, being below 21) is correctly not offered. Substituting shows only 41 works (25->13, 32->16, 65->37), so the set is exclusive but requires the substitution.
SM17A-B2.note: Ruling on the second question asked: NO, B2's option set does not admit a perfect-square filter that isolates the key. This is the one item in the batch whose OPTION-SET NOTE is an accurate description of what its set actually does. Ironically the filter it defends against is live on B3.

SM17A-B3.free_elimination: THREE struck, key isolated. (x-7)^(3/2) = 125 means sqrt(x-7) is cubed, so x - 7 must be a perfect square. Subtracting 7 from each option gives 5, 11, 18, 25 - only 25 is a perfect square, so 12, 18 and 25 all fall and 32 is the only survivor. No arithmetic beyond four mental subtractions, and no understanding of what a 3/2 exponent means is required.
SM17A-B3.note: DROP or re-option. The item carries an OPTION-SET NOTE that reasons explicitly about the set - it checks the magnitude bound (x-7 < 125) and the positivity bound and reports both inert - and misses the one filter that actually fires, which is the very filter B2 was built to defeat. That is the author declaring the bounds it had already satisfied. Fix is easy: make the distractors 7 + perfect squares (16, 23, 43, 56 style), which also kills the 'lone perfect-square offset' tell.

SM17A-B4.free_elimination: Two struck freely, a third cheaply. P(3) = P(1)*b^2 = 24b^2, so the answer must be a multiple of 24: 440 and 492 are not, and both are visibly linear-model values rather than terms of a geometric chain, so they fall on either reading. That leaves 72 = 24*3 and 216 = 24*9, and requiring b^2 to be a perfect square then isolates the key - that last step needs 648/24 = 27, so I count it as cheap rather than free. Effective floor for a solver who only knows the model is exponential is 50%. The explanation's note about the geometric mean is correct (t = 3 is not midway) but it is checking the wrong channel.
SM17A-B4.note: Weakest distractor set in the batch: two of the three distractors come from treating an explicitly exponential model as linear, which anyone who can attempt the item has already rejected. Replace 440 and 492 with values inside the multiples-of-24 family (e.g. 96, 1944) so the strike is not free.

SM17A-B5.free_elimination: Parity, one struck. The product of the zeros is 42 = 2*3*7, which carries exactly one factor of 2, so exactly one zero is even however the factorisation goes; the three pairwise products are then even, even, odd and k must be ODD. That strikes 44 - which is also, per the explanation, the option built from a triple whose product is 48, not 42. The three odd options are not separable without finding the triple.
SM17A-B5.note: Labelled medium; Vieta on a cubic plus a constrained integer-triple search is a hard-route item. Uniqueness of {2,3,7} is real and the solve snippet searches for it rather than asserting it. The 44 distractor is the weak one, both because parity kills it and because it violates the stated product; a triple with product 42 but sum not 12 would be a better trap.

SM17A-B6.free_elimination: Two struck, near-free. The inner input is 3(3) - 8 = 1, and the two branch values at x = 1 are -2 and 7 - both of which are on the list. So -41 and -3 fall as soon as the input is formed, and the item reduces to the boundary convention, a 50% floor. Separately: the key is the LONE EVEN option (-41, -3, 7 are all odd), which is the only lone-of-a-kind key in the batch - see the note.
SM17A-B6.note: Ruling on the first question asked, for this item: yes. -2 is the only even value in the set, so 'pick the one that is not like the others' lands on the key here. Low severity on its own (parity has no meaning a solver could attach to a function value, and the 50% boundary floor is the larger issue), but it is the one instance in 15 where the odd-one-out is the answer. Worth swapping one distractor to an even value, e.g. -8 for -3.

SM17A-B7.free_elimination: Two struck on integrality. The minimum is c - b^2/(4a) = 47 - 400/16, and 16 divides 400, so the minimum is an INTEGER - that strikes 2.5 and 40.75, the two non-integers, leaving -3 and 22. Recognising 16 | 400 is not really arithmetic, it is reading the coefficients. The remaining pair then splits on whether the min is positive, which needs the actual subtraction.
SM17A-B7.note: Labelled medium; completing the square on a bare quadratic with no wrapper is an easy item on the hard route. The two non-integer distractors are both strikeable as a group, so consider integer replacements (e.g. 25 for 40.75) - as set, the item is a coin flip between -3 and 22 for a solver who only checks form. Representation is fine: solve returns 22, and the decimal distractors return 2.5 and 40.75 exactly as written.

SM17A-B8.free_elimination: None found. Expanding the discriminant gives k^2 + (2m - 4a)k + (m^2 - 4an) with m = -5, a = 2, so the k-coefficient is -18 regardless of the constant term and the sum is 18 - but that derivation IS the item, not a shortcut around it. Of the options, -7 is the product of the two k-values (the constant term), which is an echo of the intermediate rather than of a printed number, and I could not strike it without forming the discriminant. Parity does not cut (three even, and the lone odd -7 is a distractor); the lone negative is likewise a distractor.
SM17A-B8.note: Correctly hard and correctly optioned. The 'exactly one real solution for exactly two values of k' phrasing is slightly heavy but unambiguous, and the explanation is right that the two k values are irrational (352 is not a perfect square) so the sum must go through the roots relation - a solver cannot back into it by testing integers.
